Figure 7.2 presents the spatiotemporal evolution of the gas phase temperature and 
selective species (n-C7H16, CH2O, O3, O2, and O) to display further insights into the 
oscillatory flame dynamics. The gas phase temperature instantaneously increases to ~1150 
K upon initiation energy deposition, consuming the initially evolved stratified fuel 
vapor/oxidizer layer. As a consequence of the rapid chemical energy heat release, the flame 
expands radially through the flammable mixture (subplot b), resulting in a gradual decrease 
in the flame temperature. To accommodate the heat transfer to the liquid to sustain 
vaporization, the flame eventually contracts and positions itself closer to the droplet surface 
having an FSR of ~ 6.5.  During this period a cool flame burn (Tmax ~710 K) is stabilized 
for a brief period of time before transitioning to a continuous the oscillatory flame mode. 
It is obvious from the XO2 distribution (subplot e, h) that ozone in the ambient initially 
dissociates (primarily via O3+N2 → O2+O+N2) from the initial ignition energy deposition 
and increases the local effective oxygen index in the region from near 0.10 to near 0.16, 
which is then maintained at that level as the system attempts to attain stable burning. As 
the burn evolves to the oscillatory mode, the peak XO2 in the surrounding is maintained at 
~ 0.14. A sharp peak in XO is also observed at a normalized radial location of ~ 20 during 
this initial phase. The peak XO radial location propagates outward as the pulsing cool flame 
regime progresses and then overlaps with the outer edge of the ozone depletion from the 
far field concentration (subplot f). For every subsequent pulse, the flame region 
progressively expands outward, a fraction of the ozone in the outer field is dissociated and 
locally increases the oxygen index. The evolution of XCH2O shows the onset of the low-
temperature kinetics and its extent during the burn time.

183 
A closer look at the XO2 and Xn-C7H16 spatiotemporal evolution (Figure 7.2 e and h) 
show the inception of the pulsing behavior. The pulsing initiates when the XO2 in the 
reaction zone (i.e., flame location based on peak temperature) approaches ~ 0.12. The local 
reduction in the oxidizer drives the flame to move outward during which unreacted XO2 
diffuses through the reaction zone toward the droplet surface. As the XO2 increases in the 
reaction zone, the flame temperature increases, the flame contracts, depleting the local XO2, 
and the cyclic process repeats. As the pulsing progress, the time of flame expansion and 
contraction increases, enabling more XO2 to diffuse through the reaction zone, which results 
in the progressive increase in Tmax in every pulse. It is interesting to note that at every pulse 
the flame continues to expand until the XO2 near the droplet surface and close to the fuel 
vapor layer reaches a value of ~ 0.11.  
To further understand the kinetic regimes affecting the oscillatory flame, the 
temperature and selective low-temperature species evolutionary profile for one complete 
cycle is presented in Figure 7.3.  A temporal window of ~0.558-0.638 s is chosen as the 
fluctuation magnitude of both temperature and species are distinctive at this stage. Figure 
7.3 illustrates Tmax and maximum mole fraction of ΣC7H14O3 and ΣC7H14  profiles. These 
two species (with cumulative isomers) are considered to represent the extent of influence 
of hydroperoxyheptyl radical (C7H14OOH) consumption stemming from the competition 
between chain propagation/termination and degenerate chain branching reactions [27]. The 
first reaction class converts C7H14OOH primarily to n-C7H14 (chain termination via HO2 
elimination) and C7H14O+OH (chain propagation). The degenerate chain branching route 
converts C7H14OOH to C7H14O3 through secondary molecular O2 addition and internal 
hydrogen abstraction. The figure indicates that Tmax decreases from a higher value of ~746

184 
K to a saddle value of ~682 K, and then increases to a higher value of ~750 K before 
entering the next cycle. The evolution of n-C7H14 species can be directly correlated to the 
temperature progression while the evolution of C7H14O3 passes through three distinct 
stages, 1 – 3. 
 
 
 
Figure 7.3 Temporal evolution of peak XC7H14O3 and Xn-C7H14 and Tmax for an oscillation cycle 
between ~0.558-0.638 s for the base case. Solid-dash line demarcates the temperature responsible 
for driving the C7H14O3 kinetics: threshold temperature for C7H14O3 kinetics. 
 
Typically, the maximum favorable temperature for O2C7H14OOH production 
hovers around 700 K at atmospheric pressure condition. As the cycle starts from a higher 
temperature, the production rate diminishes for O2C7H14OOH (precursor for C7H14O3) and 
the influence is reflected on C7H14O3 mole fraction evolution and subsequent reduction in 
heat generation via the exothermic O2C7H14OOH = C7H14O3+OH reaction class. Moreover, 
the initially high temperature starts to decompose C7H14O3 through the endothermic 
reaction class C7H14O3 = R’CHO+R’(CO)R’’+OH (stage 1). The result is a sharp decrease 
in temperature as the reaction zone cannot sustain the reaction temperature from the

185 
contribution of exothermic chain branching (QOOH = OH+QO) alone.  As a result, the 
peak n-C7H14 mole fraction also decreases with time. As the temperature drops, the slope 
of the C7H14O3 profile changes and at ~0.57 s the saddle point ‘A’ (time-coordinate) is 
reached, beyond which the C7H14O3 starts to increase (change in slope). It is understandable 
that the gas phase temperature falls below a ‘threshold value’ that supports C7H14O3 
formation. This reactivates the exothermic O2QOOH = C7H14O3+OH reaction-class and is 
reflected in the temperature slope change after ~0.58 s. Thus, the simultaneous contribution 
of heat release from both the degenerate chain branching and chain propagation routes 
enables the peak temperature to recover. This process continues up to point ‘B’ ~0.63 s 
where the temperature increases sufficiently to force  C7H14O3 production to essentially 
cease. In essence, in the pulsing regime, the kinetics processes switch back and forth 
crossing the NTC turnover temperature with every pulsation. 
The dynamic competition of chain branching and propagation/termination is also 
explored in terms of the spatiotemporal evolution of ketohydroperoxide (C7H14O3) and 
cyclic ether (C7H14O) presented in Figure 7.4, along with an inlay of the rescaled peak gas 
temperature evolution. The result of attempting to achieve a steady cool flame initially 
(r/rd<5.0) for such low-level O2 ambient is clearly visible from the quasi-steady evolution 
of both of these species. However, as the oscillation grows, the phase lag between the 
species starts to become apparent. Chain propagation reactions (QOOH = QO+OH) can be 
supported at an intermediate temperature (> 800 K) compared to C7H14O3 kinetics at 
atmospheric pressure condition. Therefore, at temperatures that exceed the necessary 
temperature condition, an increase of C7H14O and decrease/near-depletion of C7H14O3 
mole fraction is observed. The temperature response of these two important reaction classes

186 
(through their representative species peak mole fraction) has been further examined 
through analyzing the phase diagram presented in Figure 7.5. The plot covers the time span 
of the entire oscillatory behavior (t>0.125 s) excluding the dynamic initiation phase, and 
the inset illustrates the magnified view of one representative complete oscillation cycle 
(t~0.636-0.725 s). The centroid of each of the subplots indicates the inception of flame 
oscillation that then grows with time. The  C7H14O3  and C7H14O have semi-oval and 
skewed-ellipsoidal responses with temperature. The skewed nature of C7H14O clearly 
suggests that the production rate of chain propagation reaction couples with the 
temperature fluctuation and is favored at higher temperatures. On the other hand, the semi-
oval shape of  C7H14O3 denotes the presence of a phase lag and corroborates the earlier 
discussion of the three-stage temperature response over an oscillation. It also indicates that 
C7H14O3 kinetics is favored at a lower temperature. Similar response behaviors have been 
observed in [11] for a near-limit cool flame in a counterflow diffusion flame configuration. 
 
 
 
Figure 7.4. Spatiotemporal evolution of (a) XC7H14O and (b) XC7H14O3 for n-heptane droplet 
combustion (do = 0.50 mm, XO2 = 10%, XO3 = 5%, balance XN2, 1 atm). rgas/rdrop=1 denotes the 
droplet surface. A scaled peak gas temperature fluctuation is also overlaid for visual correlation of 
the species and temperature.

187 
 
 
Figure 7.5 Phase diagram summarizing the response of peak (a) XC7H14O and (b) XC7H14O3 to 
temperature over the entire oscillatory time period for the base case. The start and end of the pulsing 
regime are denoted with the closed and open circle symbol. Subplot (a) inset: magnified view at 
t~0.636-0.725 s. 
 
In the oscillatory mode of the cool flame burning, the spatial influence of the pulse 
progressively increases affecting the outer field. This is indicative of the fact that at every 
pulse, unburnt fuel and fuel fragment continue to build up in the outer region. Figure 7.6 
illustrates the Xn-C7H16 evolution over time (t~0.48-0.56 s) at three different radial locations 
with respect to the FSR. Significant amounts of fuel and other fuel-derived species diffuse 
radially outward through the flame location without being fully consumed by oxidation 
processes. As a result, a radial growth of the species distribution is observed after every 
oscillation cycle and there is a build-up of unreacted fuel fragments in the far field as time 
progresses.  For the time-window reported in Figure 7.6, ~34-46% and ~ 13-27% of the 
fuel vapor within the flame volume escapes the flame zone unreacted and appears at 
1.5xFSR and 2.0xFSR respectively. Unreacted fuel vapor and intermediate species (its

188 
derived species/products) continuously pass through the partially-oxidized cool flame 
location, and their accumulation affects the subsequent growth of the oscillatory behavior 
outside the peak maximum temperature location. 
 
 
 
Figure 7.6 Temporal evolution of n-C7H16 mole fraction over time window ~0.48-0.58 s at three 
different spatial locations for the base case. 
 
To assess the influence of ozone in the pulsing behavior, simulations were 
conducted for a range of ozone loadings. The temporal evolution of Tmax for these cases is 
summarized in Figure 7.7. It is clear that the ozone content of the ambient strongly 
influences the oscillation patterns. For an oxygen index that is lower than the LOI, the 
pulsing magnitude decreases with increasing ozone loading. In addition, the pulse 
frequency is also found to increase as the ozone fraction is increased. For a critical ozone 
level of XO3 = 6.0%, the system transitions to hot-flame burning. It can be inferred from 
the analysis that under near limit conditions (i.e. LOI) the ozone which was introduced to 
permit direct initiation of cool flame burning also perturbs the cool flame burning behavior. 
However, this perturbation effect diminishes and becomes small when larger oxygen index 
conditions are applied.

189 
 
 
Figure 7.7 Temporal evolution of peak gas temperature under different O3 mole fractions (see the 
legend) for n-C7H16 droplet (Do = 0.5 mm) combustion. Ambient condition: P = 1 atm, T = 298 K, 
XO2 = 10% with balance XN2. 
 
7.5 CONCLUDING REMARKS 
 The dynamics of near-limit cool flame burning of isolated sub-millimeter sized n-
heptane (n-C7H16) droplet (Do = 0.5 mm) has been numerically investigated under 
atmospheric pressure condition. To provide the necessary near limit constraint, the oxygen 
in the ambient was set to a value that is lower than the limiting oxygen index (LOI) criteria 
for n-C7H16 and ozone (O3) was seeded (5% v/v) to the ambient to accomplish cool flame 
initiation. Based on the detailed analysis, the following features can be drawn as 
highlighting points for this computational study. 
1. At an atmospheric O2 concentration (21%) with 5% O3 (both v/v), sub-millimeter sized 
n-C7H16 droplet attains direct initiation of cool flame upon ignition energy 
initialization. Heat feedback to the droplet surface stemming from the consequence of 
‘pre-vaporized fuel + atomic O’ reaction contributes as secondary initiation energy. 
2. For the exemplary reduced O2 case (10%), the resultant ignition energy escalates the 
local gas phase temperature ~1150 K, consuming the fuel vapor near the droplet, and

190 
simultaneously increasing the O2 mole fraction ~16% (v/v) following the 
decomposition of O3. Due to the diffusive/thermo-kinetic balance of heat generation, 
the system attains a quasi-steady cool flame burn for a brief period of time which then 
enters an ever-oscillatory low-temperature cool flame burn. 
3. It is found that within each full oscillatory cycle, the maximum local gas phase 
temperature (i.e., flame) resides closest to the droplet, and the flame positions itself to 
the furthest radial location when its value reaches the cycle minima. At each successive 
pulse, the flame region (including the reaction zone) progressively grows outward as a 
result of continuous fuel leakage through the flame location. 
4. The inception of oscillation is initiated by the local depletion of O2 below the critical 
mole fraction of 12%. This reduction of O2 compels the flame to grow outside to meet 
the O2 requirement for spherical diffusion flame. 
5. Further analyses indicate that the dynamic interaction of degenerate chain branching 
and chain termination/propagation reaction classes of QOOH associated with the low 
temperature and NTC kinetic regimes, and continuous fuel leakage across the flame 
location contribute to the ever-increasing trends of the oscillation magnitude. It is found 
that while the progression of QOOHchain propagation/termination reaction class 
directly correlates with the gas phase temperature field within a full oscillation cycle, 
the QOOHdegenerate branching reactions undergo three distinct stages within the 
same oscillation cycle. The oscillatory burning, which essentially is a perturbation 
effect resulting from the presence of ozone, is prominent under low ozone loading and 
diminishes as the ozone fraction in the system is increased.

191

CHAPTER 8 
CONCLUSION

198 
8.1 PREFACE TO CLOSURE 
Combustion of sub-millimeter sized (Do < 1.0 mm) isolated sphero-symmetric 
liquid fuel droplets has been numerically studied in this thesis work employing one-
dimensional CFD code for renewable alcohol fuels and higher n-alkanes. Methanol 
(CH3OH) and butanol (C4H9OH, including its four isomers) represent the first category of 
fuels while n-heptane (n-C7H16) and n-decane (n-C10H22) consist of the second category. 
Two major forms of flame configurations, namely high temperature and low temperature 
(including cool) flames, have been extensively studied. In this dissertation, results 
pertaining to the high-temperature flames are exclusively related to the renewable alcohol 
fuels, while the low-temperature flames are examined through the higher n-alkanes. To 
emulate the practical droplet combustion in reduced or near-absence of gravity condition, 
all the relevant physics are incorporated in the modeling formulation along with detailed 
description of kinetics. For selective case studies, experimental comparison and validation 
have also been performed on ad-hoc basis against international space station (ISS) and 
terrestrial drop-tower test data. The unified goal of this research work is to demonstrate the 
droplet combustion’s unique capabilities in relation to both the applied and scientific 
understanding of fuel combustion. Although each of the fuel has been investigated under 
the same generic computational framework, i.e., microgravity droplet combustion, the 
objectives, and consequent research findings from each study are uniquely disparate. The 
the following section discusses the main contributions and highlighting points arising from 
this research endeavor.

199 
8.2 MAJOR CONTRIBUTIONS 
a. Understanding the fire-suppression mechanism under zero-gravity environment is 
important in designing next-generation spacecraft fire safety protocols. Practically 
speaking, it is also very relevant to the existing space programs in relation to 
inadvertent fire hazards. Therefore, the necessity to assess the effectiveness of different 
fire-suppressant mediums is critical. However, testing these suppressants under the g~0 
condition is logistically challenging and expensive. In this thesis, it has been 
demonstrated that the computational droplet combustion study can contribute to 
predicting the fire-extinguishment behavior of any untested gaseous suppressant. An 
exemplary case has been reported for xenon (Xe) in chapter 3, the-then considered as 
a potential fire extinguisher for space application by the National Aeronautics and 
Astronautics Agency (NASA). Through exhaustive numerical calculations, it has been 
unambiguously shown that xenon underperforms compared to other existing fire-
suppressants due to its uniquely low thermal diffusivity. As a direct contribution from 
our research effort, NASA also realized the possible drawbacks of xenon as a micro-
gravity fire suppressant and postponed testing and investing resources on it. 
b. Robust design of the chemical kinetic model is an intrinsically necessary part of 
numerical computations for reacting systems. Therefore, the predictive reliability of 
simulation directly depends on the accuracy and fidelity of the kinetic model itself. In 
this dissertation, through chapters 4-5, it has been manifested that droplet combustion 
simulation can be utilized as an effective tool for model validation and refinement. 
Furthermore, it has also been demonstrated that droplet combustion can surpass the 
validation capabilities of the traditional gas-phase unsteady homogenous and steady

200 
transport dependent experimental targets. As a benchmark study, the combustion 
chemistry of butanol and its isomer are considered, and two detailed models (Sarathy 
et al. 2012, Marchent et al. 2013) have been tested for this purpose against ground base 
drop tower droplet combustion test data. The initial validation exercise highlighted that 
the Sarathy et al. model predicted an accelerated fuel burning for butanol isomers, 
leading us to investigate the primary reason for such anomaly behavior. Through 
meticulous computational rigor via droplet combustion, the inherent source of the 
inconsistency for Saraty et al. model has been identified. Following the 
recommendations from our studies to update fuel specific transport parameters, the 
model was revised by its authors, the prediction performances improved significantly 
for both gas and liquid phase targets. 
c. The low-temperature kinetic behavior of straight chain paraffinic fuels is unique due to 
their negative temperature coefficient (NTC) response. And, within the NTC range of 
temperature, cool flame for droplet is defined as the low-temperature chemistry-driven 
flame that can support maximum burning rate at a given ambient (P, T) and constraint 
by the transport phenomena, i.e. diffusive loss/gain. Because of its applied importance 
to engine knock and ignition in spark and compression ignition engines respectively, 
and potential for homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) engines, the cool 
flame has been widely studied in recent years under diversified experimental and 
computational platforms. However, considering its practical relevance to multiphase 
spray arrangement, cool flame for sub-millimeter sized droplets has neither been 
explored experimentally nor computationally. Here, we have advanced the 
understanding of ozone assisted (O3) directly initiated smaller fuel droplet (Do = 0.5

201 
mm) cool flame by employing CFD simulation with detailed kinetics. The mechanistic 
features of such direct establishment of cool flame are thoroughly explained to 
encourage the experimental researchers to conduct tests on ground-based drop tower 
test facilities. In addition, the oscillatory behavior of such smaller droplet cool flame is 
further investigated to elucidate the kinetic competitions (i.e., pathways) responsible 
for such oscillatory flame behavior.  
 
8.3 FUTURE RECOMMENDATIONS 
 The strength of the current version of isolated droplet combustion CFD code stems 
from the simplicity of low dimensional flow field that augments the coupling of large 
kinetics and other associated thermo-fluid sub-models.  To further transcend its capability, 
the following recommendations are provided in light of the experiences harnessed through 
the course of this dissertation work. The author believes that each of the three proposals 
reported here could be a Ph.D. and/or M.S. level research topic by their own prospect for 
future exploration.  
a. Sooting fuel simulation. To model the sooting fuels, currently, the CFD code has 
two versions of soot model, namely- the BIN method [1] and the moment method 
[2]. Both of these soot modeling methods are fairly detailed in nature, therefore the 
simulation complexity increases tremendously when coupled with detailed gas 
phase kinetics. A potential way forward to address the soot modeling for droplet 
combustion is to incorporate semi-detailed soot modeling [3] to reduce the 
simulation turn over time.

202 
b. The inclusion of real gas formulation. The ideal gas law is a typically the default 
choice for the equation of states (EOS) for most of the available commercial and 
in-house legacy codes. This simplified formulation of EOS is found to work 
satisfactorily at ambient and above ambient pressures for both the reacting and non-
reacting CFD simulations. However, ideal gas law starts to underperform 
significantly as the gas phase system approaches critical pressure regime for the 
species of interests. Therefore, to address this concern, the real gas effect should be 
included and the overall code structure has to be updated and validated against 
experimental targets accordingly. 
c. Multi-dimensional effect.  Although the one-dimensional droplet combustion is 
simple in terms of fluid physics, it is relevant to the complex spray combustion by 
incorporating moving boundary effects, unsteady heat transfer, mass diffusion to 
and from the droplet surface, temperature dependent variable properties, phase 
equilibrium at the interface and radiative perturbation. In order to progress towards 
real spray arrangement without compromising in terms of kinetic aspect, the next 
step should be to include multi-dimensional effect for isolated droplet combustion. 
With this end in view, the influence of gravity, external convective perturbation 
and heat and mass transfer among multiple droplets should be considered.

203

Abstract
Large carbon number
n
-alkanes are a notable component in all real transportation fuels, and their chemical structure fosters substantial low temperature kinetic reactivity. Normal alkanes have been studied in various canonical configurations but rarely in systems with strong coupling between low temperature chemistry and transport for pure as well as for multi-component
n
-alkane mixtures. The
Fl
ame
Ex
tinguishment (FLEX) experiments onboard the International Space Station provided a unique platform for investigating low temperature multi-phase
n
-alkane and
iso
-alkane combustion. Among the many interesting phenomena experimentally observed, cool flame extinction can occur, accompanied by the concurrent formation of a surrounding cloud of condensed vapor. In this work we conduct numerical simulations of high and low temperature combustion of large, initially single-component
n
-heptane,
n
-decane and
n
-dodecane droplets. The role of initial droplet diameter, operating pressure, and
n
-alkyl carbon number on the extinction of hot and low temperature flames is investigated and compared against the available experimental data. While all three fuels exhibit similar hot flame behavior, cool flame activity increases with the carbon number, resulting in an increased cool flame temperature and decreased extinction diameter. Multi-cyclic “hot/cool flame transitions” are found in air as pressure is slightly increased above one atmosphere. The cyclic behaviors correspond to continuously varying hot and cool flame transitions across the high, low, and negative temperature coefficient (NTC) kinetic regimes. Further increase in pressure results in a second stage steady “
Warm flame
” transition. The extinction of hot and cool flame has a strong non-linear dependence on ambient pressure but as the hot flame extinction diameter increases with pressure the extinction diameter of the cool flame decreases. The computational results are compared with a recent asymptotic analysis of FLEX
n
-alkane cool flames.

Abstract
Isolated droplet burning behaviors of fuel mixtures that all share the fully pre-vaporized combustion behaviors of the same “global” Jet-A real fuel are investigated numerically to elucidate the effects of preferential vaporization. Predictions are generated using three such multi-component hydrocarbon mixtures (Mixture-1: n-decane/iso-octane/toluene 42.7/33.0/24.3, Mixture-2: n-dodecane/iso-octane/1,3,5 trimethyl benzene 49.0/21.0/30.0 and Mixture-3: n-hexadecane/iso-octane/1,3,5 trimethyl benzene 36.5/31.0/32.5 molar ratios), each having very different distillation properties. Simulations are performed using a transient one-dimensional sphero-symmetric model, involving numerically reduced detailed chemical kinetics, and multi-component gas-phase diffusive transport. The interactions among the different liquid-phase components are modeled using UNIFAC activity coefficient methodology. The predictions using Mixture-1 are found to be in good agreement with previously published drop-tower experiments for 550 µm droplet combustion in air. Stagnant and internally mixed liquid-phase behaviors are both considered. Near fully mixed internal conditions and including sooting effects (observed in the experiments) result in predictions that are in good agreement with experimental drop diameter and flame-standoff ratio histories. By comparing predictions for the three mixtures, preferential vaporization effects exhibit strong non-linear dependences on initial droplet diameter and ambient pressure. At low pressures and for droplet sizes typical of those found in multi-phase gas turbine combustors, comparable diffusion and vaporization characteristic times favor frozen limit vaporization. However, at pressures typical of those found in applications, batch distillation dominates and preferential vaporization chemical property differences are found to become as significant as physical property effects in influencing combustion behaviors.

Abstract
Cool flames play a critical role in ignition timing, burning rate, burning limits, engine knocking, and emissions in conventional and advanced combustion engines. This paper provides an overview of the recent progress in experimental and computational studies of cool flames. First, a brief review of low-temperature chemistry and classical studies of cool flames is presented. Next, the recent experimental and computational findings of cool flames in microchannels, microgravity droplet combustion, counterflow flames, and turbulent combustion environments are reviewed. The flammability diagrams of different low-temperature flames and their relations to hot flames in premixed and nonpremixed systems are discussed. The impact of cool flames on turbulent combustion and knock formation is also highlighted. Finally, future avenues in cool flame research, including the use of cool flames as a new platform for low-temperature kinetic model validation, are presented. It is concluded that the understanding and control of low-temperature combustion is critical for the development of future advanced engines and new fuels.

Abstract
Transient, isolated
n
-alkane droplet combustion is simulated at elevated pressure for helium-diluent substituted-air mixtures. We report the presence of unique quasi-steady, three-stage burning behavior of large sphero-symmetric
n
-alkane droplets at these elevated pressures and helium substituted ambient fractions. Upon initiation of reaction, hot-flame diffusive burning of large droplets is initiated that radiatively extinguishes to establish cool flame burning conditions in nitrogen/oxygen “air” at atmospheric and elevated pressures. However, at elevated pressure and moderate helium substitution for nitrogen (
X
He
> 20%), the initiated cool flame burning proceeds through two distinct, quasi-steady-state, cool flame burning conditions. The classical “
Hot flame
” (∼1500 K) radiatively extinguishes into a “
Warm flame
” burning mode at a moderate maximum reaction zone temperature (∼ 970 K), followed by a transition to a lower temperature (∼765 K), quasi-steady “
Cool flame
” burning condition. The reaction zone (“flame”) temperatures are associated with distinctly different yields in intermediate reaction products within the reaction zones and surrounding near-field, and the flame-standoff ratios characterizing each burning mode progressively decrease. The presence of all three stages first appears with helium substitution near 20%, and the duration of each stage is observed to be strongly dependent on helium substitutions level between 20–60%. For helium substitution greater than 60%, the hot flame extinction is followed by only the lower temperature cool flame burning mode. In addition to the strong coupling between the diffusive loss of both energy and species and the slowly evolving degenerate branching in the low and negative temperature coefficient (NTC) kinetic regimes, the competition between the low-temperature chain branching and intermediate-temperature chain termination reactions control the “
Warm”
and “
Cool
” flame quasi-steady conditions and transitioning dynamics. Experiments onboard the International Space Station with
n
-dodecane droplets confirm the existence of these combustion characteristics and predictions agree favorably with these observations.

Abstract
This paper presents data from large, isolated n-dodecane droplets burning in microgravity on the International Space Station, along with preliminary comparisons with numerical and analytic predictions indicating general agreement in trends. The tests involved were primarily in air (a few in reduced oxygen) at ambient pressures ranging from 0.50 to 5.0 atm. After ignition, the droplets burn with a hot flame that extinguishes when the radiant energy loss causes the flame temperature to drop below the hot-flame-required value. The total flame radiative loss at extinction is nearly independent of pressure, while the peak flame diameter prior to hot-flame extinction decreases with increasing pressure. The maximum hot-flame temperature, inferred from fiber-support radiative emisssions, decreases with increasing pressure, and the hot flames become dimmer with increasing pressure. At 1.0 atm and below there is a prolonged period of coolflame burning that ends with cool-flame extinction at a finite droplet size; the cool-flame-extinction droplet diameter increases and the cool-flame burning rate decreases with decreasing ambient pressure. Above 1.25 atm warm-flame burning and hot-flame re-ignitions become prevalent. At 5.0 atm, there is no abrupt hot-flame extinction with transition to a cool flame; the flame gradually gets dimmer, and the flame temperature decreases over a much longer time, the transition between hot-flame and warm-flame burning becoming almost undiscernible.

Introduction
The first observations of cool flames date back to 1817 (Davy
1817
). Subsequent to the initial discovery of cool flames, cool flame research advanced owing to the importance of low-temperature chemistry in engines, and in particular, engine knock. Advanced engine concepts such as homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) and reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI) engines have the potential for increased efficiency and reduced emissions by increasing operating pressures and lowering operating temperatures; placing more importance on a predictive understanding of low-temperature chemical kinetics. Traditionally most cool-flame research utilized premixed fuel/air mixtures in static (e.g., Mallard and Le Chatelier
1880
) and flow (e.g., Dryer and Glassman
1973
) reactors, rapid compression machines (e.g., Sung and Curran
2014
) and shock tubes (e.g., Hanson and Davidson
2014
; Herbon et al.
2002
). An important concept in cool-flame research is the presence of the negative temperature coefficient (NTC) regime where, at an intermediate temperature range between the cold starting condition and the hot-flame temperature, the overall reactivity (heat release) decreases with increasing temperature.
As highlighted by Law and Faeth (Law and Faeth
1994
), reduced-gravity studies offer geometric simplification (e.g., 1-D flames), and no buoyant flows which allow the study of weak, near-limit flames which include cool flames. Kumagai and Isoda (
1956
) were the first to realize the advantages of the microgravity environment experimentally by studying spherically-symmetric droplet combustion in a one second drop tower at the University of Tokyo. Pearlman and co-workers (Fairlie et al.
2005
; Foster and Pearlman
2006
; Pearlman
2000
), however, were the first to recognize the potential for microgravity studies to provide a window into cool flame research by eliminating the buoyancy-induced flows associated with the low-temperature heat release. The authors used a static reactor and showed how the buoyant flows changes both the flame shape and evolution and cool-flame induction time.
Prior to 2012 most droplet combustion research in microgravity involved the ignition, burning and extinction of ‘hot flames’, with flame temperatures greater than or equal to approximately 1200 K (e.g., Nayagam et al.
1998
). There was a limited amount of research that examined low-temperature chemistry during two-stage ignition of isolated droplets in ambient temperatures below about 900 K (Tanabe et al.
1995
). Studies of large alkane droplets in a long-duration experiment (FlammabilityLimit-Experiment, FLEX) on the International Space Station (ISS) showed, for the first time, quasi-steady droplet combustion sustained by a low temperature or cool flame (Nayagam et al.
2012
; Farouk and Dryer
2014
; Cuoci et al.
2013
). This cool-flame supported droplet burning is possible because of the existence of the NTC regime.
Following the discovery of cool-flame burning in the ISS experiments Ju and coworkers were able to sustain steady cool flames in terrestrial laboratory studies using a counter-flow burner. The initial experiments (Reuter et al.
2016
,
2017a
) used dimethyl ether (DME) and ozone to promote the low-temperature burning. Subsequent experiments, however, used alkane fuels, first with ozone in the oxidizer stream and finally with no ozone (Reuter et al.
2017b
) to produce a cool diffusion flame. Unlike the ISS experiments that have limited resources (i.e., test points and test time), these terrestrial counter-flow experiments provided a detailed flammability map for cool flames across a wide range of fuels and ambient conditions (Reuter et al.
2017b
). These observations of stable cool diffusion flames have given researchers a wealth of insights into cool flame behavior and led to an improved predictive capability of cool-flame behavior; these insights compiled and summarized in recent review articles (Ju
2021
; Ju et al.
2019
).
Cool-flame droplet burning in the FLEX experiments occurred when the hot-flame (ignited by a heated wire) surrounding a large alkane fuel droplet extinguished when the radiative loss from the flame reduced the temperature below that required to sustain combustion (e.g., Dietrich et al.
2014
; Nayagam et al.
1998
; Marchese et al.
1999
). This hot-flame extinction then led to a prolonged period of quasi-steady low-temperature burning characterized by a linear d-squared (droplet-diameter-time) regression and a near-constant flame-standoff ratio (Farouk and Dryer
2014
; Nayagam et al.
2016
). Subsequent FLEX experiments showed that the hot flame is not strictly necessary to achieve cool-flame burning; the cool flame ignition can occur by raising the flash point of the fuel using a much lower ignition energy so as to not overheat the liquid and produce a significant diffusive fuel vapor/air layer around the droplet (Farouk et al.
2017
). The FLEX experiments further showed that the cool flame burns only a fraction of the vaporized fuel, and the unburned fuel re-condenses far outside the flame zone to form a large vapor cloud that is visible on both a backlit view of the droplet and a color camera view of the experiment (Dietrich et al.
2017a
,
b
). When the droplet becomes small enough, the cool flame extinguishes, a process that is characterized by a plateau in the droplet regression history and rapid condensation of the remaining fuel vapor (Nayagam et al.
2015
).
The FLEX experiments also showed the significant influence of pressure on cool-flame droplet burning. The first experiments at hyperbaric pressures and related numerical modeling showed that, in carbon-dioxide-diluted atmospheres, the cool flame could spontaneously re-ignite a hot flame that would subsequently extinguish and initiate further cool-flame burning, a process that could repeat itself multiple times (Farouk et al.
2015
). Subsequent experiments and numerical modeling showed that this process can occur at lower pressures and does not require ambient carbon dioxide (Dietrich et al.
2017a
,
b
; Farouk and Dryer
2022
). Further FLEX experiments and companion modeling (Farouk et al.
2019
) with n-heptane fuel droplets at elevated (3 atm) pressure in helium-diluted ambient environments found that following hot-flame extinction the flame transitions to a ‘warm-flame’ burning mode where the flame temperature is around 970 K for a short period, and then moves into a ‘cool-flame’ mode with a lower flame temperature (∼ 765 K). Independently Ju and co-workers (Yehia et al.
2018
,
2019
) also showed the existence of warm diffusion flames on experiments with their counter-flow burner.
This article presents experimental results of the Cool-Flames-Investigation (CFI) experiments aboard the ISS that studied the low-temperature droplet burning in more detail. The experiments used a new camera system to visualize the cool flame, a variable-gain radiometer, and different fuels and fuel mixtures. The test conditions focused on oxygen/nitrogen mixtures over a range of pressures, including a limited number of tests at the same oxygen index but with helium replacing some of the inert (nitrogen). The present paper summarizes all of the experimental results for n-dodecane in oxygen/nitrogen ambients. Farouk and Dryer (
2022
) presented some of the data earlier in numerical modeling and analyses of hot- and cool-flame burning and extinction phenomena; this work emphasizes the experimental observations and includes radiometer and sooting data not yet available in the literature.
Experimental Apparatus and Data Analysis
The experiments used the Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) that is an insert to the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), a full-sized rack inside the Destiny module of the ISS. The hardware and software are identical to that in previous publications (Dietrich et al.
2014
,
2015a
,
b
), except for some important differences. The field-of-view (FOV) of the backlit images of the droplet was increased to approximately 5 cm × 5 cm but used the same image array (1024 × 1024 pixels). This resulted in slightly less spatial resolution but increased the likelihood that a free-floating droplet would stay in the FOV. The recent experiments also used a new intensified camera (12-bit, 1392 × 1040 monochrome pixel array) equipped with a filter wheel and an increased FOV (90 mm × 68 mm). For the hot-flame burning period a filter wheel rotates to place a narrowband 430 nm filter in front of the camera and lens to visualize the
CH
∗
chemiluminescence. When the radiometer detects hot-flame extinction, the filter wheel rotates to put a wideband (390–490 nm) filter in front of the camera so that it can detect the formaldehyde chemiluminescence from the cool flame.
There was a protection system for the camera that shut down the intensifier when the camera and radiometer detected a hot-flame re-ignition during cool-flame burning. This system worked quite well at lower pressures. At higher ambient pressures, however, it became more complex as the hot flames became dimmer, the warm flames brighter and re-ignitions were frequent and unpredictable. As a result there were periods of the test where there was no image data from the intensified camera because either the wrong filter was in place and/or the camera shut down because of a hot-flame re-ignition.
The droplets in the previous FLEX experiments were primarily free-floated in the chamber. Some experiments, however, ‘tethered’ the droplet to an 80 µm silicon-carbide (SiC) fiber to maintain all of the events within the FOV of all of the cameras. This tethering significantly increased the likelihood of a successful test, but led to perturbations in the burning process, especially at small droplet diameters, such as near cool-flame extinction. To further reduce perturbations to the burning process, the present experiments used a smaller 40 µm carbide fiber to tether the droplet.
To improve flame radiation observations, the fixed-gain amplification used in the prior FLEX experiments was replaced by a variable-gain amplifier to better resolve the flame radiance during both the hot-flame and cool-flame burning periods. This modification was especially important for recording the narrowband radiometer observations (looking at water vapor emission in the 5–7 µm range) at both cool- and hot-flame burning conditions without saturating the amplifier.
Finally, software modifications were implemented to better control the energy supplied to the droplet during the ignition phase of each experiment. Whereas the previous ISS droplet-combustion experiments used a preset ignition time, the current experiments used feedback from the radiometers to determine when ignition of the developing fuel vapor/oxidizer layer occurred. Once the radiometer detected flame initiation, the control computer turned off the igniters and retracted them from the droplet automatically. The radiometer values chosen to indicate ignition and extinction of the hot flame were set by the test operators prior to each experiment and could be changed from test to test.
The fuel for the results presented in this article was pure n-dodecane and the ambient gas mixtures were oxygen/nitrogen (0.21/0.79 and 0.17/0.83
O
2
/N
2
mole fraction). The ambient pressure ranged from 0.50 to 5.0 atm; the higher pressures representing a change from the previous FLEX experiments that were limited to 3.0 atm. In theory the experiments could have used droplet diameters from approximately 1 mm to over 7 mm based on previous ISS droplet combustion experiments. Droplets smaller than 3–3.5 mm tend to burn to completion and do not exhibit radiative hot-flame extinction and cool-flame burning. Larger droplets, however, use large amounts of fuel and have very long test times (thus consuming large amounts of digital storage and requiring long downlink times). As a result, with a few exceptions, all of the tests used initial droplet sizes in the 4–5 mm range.
The cool flames from the ISS droplet combustion experiments are very dim, invisible to the color video camera on the MDCA and barely discernible with the intensified camera. The images improve with median filtering and image-averaging over 500 ms (Nayagam et al.
2016
). Automated image-processing procedures provide a measure of the flame diameter from a line profile across the center of the flame. Reported here are two relevant measures of the cool flame, the peak-to-peak flame diameter representing the diameter of peak chemiluminescence and a full-width, half-max (FWHM) diameter that represents the outer diameter of the flame where the grayscale value of the flame chemiluminescence reaches one half the peak value.
Model Descriptions
Numerical Model
The mathematical model employed to describe the transient vaporization, flame initiation, and combustion histories of isolated pure and multi-component fuel droplets in the high-, intermediate-, and low-temperature regimes under microgravity conditions uses the numerical model described in detail in previous works (Alam et al.
2019
; Farouk et al.
2021
; Farouk and Dryer
2014
). The model solves the conservation equations for mass, species, and energy for both the liquid and gas phases assuming spherical symmetry. It includes both Fickian and Soret diffusion for evaluating multicomponent species diffusion velocities in the gas phase. A statistical narrow-band radiation model is employed to obtain spectral radiative effects. The model is also capable of resolving the thermal perturbation resulting from tethering fibers (Farouk and Dryer
2011
). Liquid-phase property data are taken from the Daubert and Danner database (Daubert and Danner
1989
). A comprehensive detailed kinetic model consisting of 583 species and 2609 reactions (Sarathy et al.
2011
) describes the gas-phase chemical reactions of n-dodecane and is a construct developed for n-alkanes covering a carbon number range from
C
7
-
C
20
. The mechanism resolves the high, intermediate and low-temperature kinetic regimes for n-dodecane. The far field is typically two hundred times the initial droplet diameter with Dirichlet boundary conditions for fixed ambient composition and temperature. The numerical model formulation does not include consideration of soot formation.
The spatial discretization is a node-centered finite-volume scheme with second-order accuracy. Time discretization is a backward-difference formula, up to fifth order, with a variable time step, making it a fully implicit multipoint interpolation scheme. The complete set of coupled partial differential and algebraic equations are discretized first in space and then integrated in time in an automated fashion as a set of coupled ordinary differential–algebraic equations. This approach is appropriate for the large range of time scales and stability constraints imposed by the current chemically reacting system. The numerical scheme can resolve the flame dynamics associated with ignition and extinction as well as re-ignition efficiently without compromising computation time.

The results show that the cool-flame burning-rate constant increases continuously from the lowest pressure tested (0.50 atm) to approximately 3 atm. The limited data from 3 - 5 atm suggest that the burning-rate constant is relatively constant. Above 2 atm, however, it may not be appropriate to call it the cool-flame burning-rate constant as in this region the droplet burns in the warm-flame regime which is characterized by flames that are closer in size to the hot flame, with flame radiances (broadband) that are also closer to those of the hot-flame radiance. In addition, the hot-flame re-ignitions from the cool/warm flames frequently occur at ambient pressures of 2 atm and above. The burning-rate constants in Fig.
4

The numerical simulations show that for pressures higher than 2.5 atm the flame, after the radiative extinction of the hot flame, transitions to a quasi-steady warm flame and burns to completion. The predicted average burning rate in the 2.5 - 5.0 atm pressure range represents the warm-flame burn as no cool-flame burning takes place in this pressure range. The predicted average burning rate as a function of pressure over the entire range is highly nonlinear and clearly shows the presence of the two apparently distinct regimes. These two regimes are characterized by the two different slopes, although the data are not extensive enough to verify that, given the experimental uncertainties producing scatter. In the pressure range of 0.50 - 1.25 atm the average burning rate increases sharply as a function of pressure; this is the cool-flame burning regime. As the pressure increases to 2.0 atm and higher the droplet burns in the warm-flame regime. The average burning rate in the warm-flame regime is higher than that of the cool-flame regime but is less sensitive to pressure, which is apparent in a relatively weaker slope of burning rate as a function of pressure in the 2 - 5 atm range. The cool-flame analytical predictions, although closer to the data than the numerical results in an overall sense, exhibit a noticeably smaller slope than the numerical and experimental results, suggesting the need for further attention to predicted pressure dependence in future analytical studies.

Sooting Behavior
The CFI tests also reveal the significant influence of ambient pressure on the sooting behavior of both the cool and hot flames. Figure
10
shows the backlit view of the droplet at the mid-points of both the hot-flame and cool-flame burning periods for the range of pressures tested. Following ignition there is a pronounced soot shell that forms around the droplet at ambient pressures less than or equal to 2 atm. This soot shell gets more dense and moves closer to the droplet as the ambient pressure increases. At the two pressures tested above 2 atm the soot shell becomes more of a cloud that surrounds the droplet and nearly obscures the droplet surface in the backlit images.

The soot shell forms because of the balance of the Stefan drag force pushing the soot away from the droplet and the thermophoretic force on the soot particles that pulls the soot towards the droplet. At low pressures, following hot-flame extinction, the soot shell gets pushed away from the droplet into the quiescent ambient atmosphere because the thermophoretic force essentially disappears with the hot flame. As pressure increases, the drag force decreases because the magnitude of the Stefan-flow velocity decreases. In addition, the warm flame may introduce a thermophoretic force (owing to its increased temperature and larger diameter) on the soot that increases with pressure, resulting in a soot cloud that can remain close to the droplet at higher pressures.
The backlit images near hot-flame extinction (e.g., Fig.
2
d) suggest little formation of soot after that formed immediately after ignition. In addition, the color camera images show luminous radiation from soot to be completely absent at hot-flame radiative extinction (the flames are entirely blue). Neglecting soot formation during the hot-flame burning period is therefore a reasonable assumption in the numerical model. For cool-flame burning less than 2 atm pressure there is no soot in the vicinity of the droplet (Fig.
10
) as it gets pushed away from the droplet by the initial hot flame and subsequent cool flame Stefan flow. Therefore neglecting soot formation during cool-flame burning at 2 atm pressure and below is also a reasonable assumption. At higher pressures, however, the cool/warm-flame burning is more complex, and sooting may be present and how it impacts burning is more uncertain.
Discussion
This data documents the significant influence of the ambient pressure on the low-temperature-burning regime of n-dodecane droplets. At pressures less than or equal to one
atm
, in the experiments there is a prolonged period of cool-flame burning following radiative extinction of the hot flame that ends when the cool flame extinguishes at a finite droplet extinction diameter. This droplet diameter increases with decreasing ambient pressure. This process is currently understood by both numerical (e.g., Farouk and Dryer
2022
) and analytical (e.g., Nayagam et al.
2015
) treatments of the droplet combustion problem.
At pressures greater than 1.25 atm, the droplet burning after hot-flame extinction becomes more complex as hot-flame re-ignitions and warm-flame burning can all occur, and the behavior is less predictable. One particularly noteworthy aspect is the transition from a hot flame to a cool/warm flame at high pressures. Figure
11
shows the importance of ambient pressure on this transition with tests at 0.50 and 5.0 atm plotted. The CIR had another black-and-white camera that had a near-infrared filter to visualize the luminescence of the fiber during fiber-supported tests. Previous FLEX experiments (Dietrich et al.
2015a
,
b
) used this camera to obtain peak gas-phase temperatures for fiber-supported decane/hexanol droplets. The present experiments used a different filter that allowed detection of lower-temperature flames, but this also meant the ground calibration from the previous FLEX tests was no longer valid so data are presented here only on camera grayscale and not absolute temperature. Figure
11
also compares numerical simulations of both the FLEX-1238 and FLEX-1260 tests to the experimental data.

Peak fiber grayscale value, flame diameter (from the IR fiber images) and total flame radiance for exemplar droplets at 0.50 and 5.0 atm. The lines show predictions from a detailed numerical model (Farouk and Dryer
2022
). The graph shows only a sparse subset of the experimental data for clarity
Figure
11
shows the total peak fiber luminescence, flame diameter (using the distance between the peaks of where the flame impinges on the fiber) and total flame radiance as functions of time for the droplets at two different pressures. Consistent with the data in Fig.
6
, the graph shows that the hot-flame diameter is significantly smaller at 5.0 atm than at 0.50 atm. At 0.50 atm the flame radiance rises quickly and reaches peak value near 25 W, and it remains near that value until hot-flame extinction, after which it quickly drops to a value less that 5 W during cool-flame burning.
The experiment and numerical prediction clearly show the hot-flame-to-cool-flame transition for the 0.50 atm test. The peak hot-flame radiance is predicted to be approximately 30 W, higher than the measured value. The predicted flame-diameter temporal evolution follows the experimental trajectory reasonably well, with the transition to cool-flame burning taking place at approximately 15 s, about 4 s later than the measured value. During the quasi-steady cool-flame burning the model predicts a flame radiance of approximately 3 W, which agrees favorably with the measurements. During low-temperature burning the flame maintains a flame diameter of approximately 10 mm. The flame-temperature evolution shows that during the early stage of high-temperature burning the temperature decreases sharply and then approaches a quasi-steady condition prior to the transition to cool-flame burning. The model predicts a peak hot-flame temperature of approximately 1170 K just prior to the transition to cool-flame burning and a nearly constant peak temperature of approximately 740 K during cool-flame burning.
The test at 5.0 atm is completely different. The flame-diameter, flame-radiance and peak-fiber-grayscale data show no clear transition between hot-flame burning and warm-flame burning. The peak fiber grayscale is saturated initially and shows a continuous decrease after ignition, with some small hot-flame re-ignitions before it reaches a steady value (constant peak flame temperature) during warm-flame burning. The flame-diameter and flame-radiance data also show a smooth transition, with some perturbations associated with minor hot-flame re-ignitions. Previous FLEX testing showed that as pressure increases the hot flames get progressively dimmer (Dietrich et al.
2017a
,
b
). This was also true in the CFI dodecane tests presented here. At the lower pressures, the hot flames viewed with the intensified camera and color camera were relatively easy to track and identify. At higher pressures, however, the hot flames became almost invisible in both cameras.
Unlike the experiments, the simulation clearly shows a transition in the flame radiance and flame diameter evolution between hot- and warm-flame burning. In the first stage the model predicts a maximum hot-flame radiance of approximately 40 W, which then reduces to approximately 18 W in the second, warm-flame stage. The flame diameter reaches a peak value of about 25 mm and then reduces to around 19 mm as the system proceeds to warm-flame burning. The variation in both the flame radiance and flame diameter between the transitions is much smaller at 5.0 atm than it is at 0.50 atm. The temperature predictions clearly show that at 5.0 atm pressure the temporal change of the peak flame temperature is slower than at 0.50 atm, but a quasi-steady hot flame is never achieved. It is interesting to note that the transition from the hot to warm flame at 5.0 atm occurs at approximately 1096 K which is similar to the value predicted for 0.50 atm. In comparison to the 0.50 atm case, where the transition from hot- to cool-flame burning happens abruptly, the hot- to warm-flame transition occurs relatively slowly at 5.0 atm. The change in the temperature during the hot- to warm-flame transition is also small at 5.0 atm, with a quasi-steady warm-flame temperature of about 1000 K. The smaller nature of the change may be one of the reasons that the differences between the experiments and predictions are not discernible.
Kinetically, an increase in the operating pressure results in an increase in both the turnover temperature into the NTC regime and hot ignition-temperature transition associated with hydrogen-peroxide decomposition, at the terminus of the NTC temperature regime. The difference in the reactivity between the two temperatures, however, decreases with increasing pressure. The warm flame is dictated by the NTC kinetics and a competition for
OH

. Since the flame radius during warm-flame burning is much larger than that during cool-flame burning (e.g., Fig.

) and the flame temperatures are higher, radiative losses become more significant during warm-flame burning. The radiative heat loss decreases the flame temperature, but the diffusive losses of species are insufficient to slow down the NTC reactions that define the heat-generation time scale. As a result, the peak temperature in the warm flame initially decreases from about 1050 K to 990 K and then increases back to about 1055 K. Despite the variation in the flame temperature, the warm-flame burning rate continually decreases, albeit slowly.
Conclusions
This paper presented comprehensive data from large, isolated n-dodecane droplet combustion experiments in microgravity conducted aboard the ISS. The experiments were primarily in air (with a few tests at reduced oxygen) and ambient pressures ranging from 0.50 to 5.0 atm. The experiments show the significant impact of pressure on cool- and warm-flame burning with cool-flame burning and extinction observed at lower pressures following hot-flame radiative extinction. At higher pressures warm-flame burning and hot-flame re-ignition became more prevalent. The experimental observations were quantified by measurements of the droplet burning rate, extinction droplet diameters, flame diameters and flame radiative energy loss.
Detailed numerical modeling shows good agreement with the experiments particularly at lower pressures. The (small) disagreement between the model and experiments at these pressures is likely the result of experimental uncertainties, inaccuracies in the low and intermediate temperature chemistry models and physical effects, such as fuel (and large fuel fragments) vapor condensation (Williams et al.
2021
), not included in the model formulation. At higher pressures the experiments became less repeatable with spontaneous hot-flame re-ignitions that made measurements of droplet burning rate, flame size and radiative energy loss more difficult. Despite the lack of a large data set at higher pressures (large number of tests to develop statistical confidence and error bands) the model still does a reasonable job in predicting both qualitatively and quantitatively the experimental observations.
The data from the CFI experiments are beneficial in the development and validation of numerical models of low and intermediate chemistry in a more realistic (diffusive, two-phase system), but geometrically simple (spherically symmetric) combustion system. The CFI experiments also included tests (not reported in this paper) that examined how fuel structure influenced cool- and warm-flame burning. These tests involved dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures as well as tests with farnesane (a sustainable aviation fuel) and the data is publicly available (psi.ndc.nasa.gov) and will be the subject of subsequent publications by the authors. Future experiments that have more detailed diagnostics would enable a more detailed comparison between model predictions.

Low Temperature n‑Dodecane Droplet Combustion Experiments 
Aboard the International Space Station
Daniel Dietrich1 · Timmothy Krause2 · Vedha Nayagam3 · Tanvir Farouk4 · Frederick Dryer4 · Forman Williams5
Received: 7 December 2023 / Accepted: 18 April 2024 / Published online: 13 May 2024 
This is a U.S. Government work and not under copyright protection in the US; foreign copyright protection may apply 2024
Abstract
This paper presents data from large, isolated n-dodecane droplets burning in microgravity on the International Space Station, 
along with preliminary comparisons with numerical and analytic predictions indicating general agreement in trends. The 
tests involved were primarily in air (a few in reduced oxygen) at ambient pressures ranging from 0.50 to 5.0 atm. After igni-
tion, the droplets burn with a hot flame that extinguishes when the radiant energy loss causes the flame temperature to drop 
below the hot-flame-required value. The total flame radiative loss at extinction is nearly independent of pressure, while the 
peak flame diameter prior to hot-flame extinction decreases with increasing pressure. The maximum hot-flame temperature, 
inferred from fiber-support radiative emisssions, decreases with increasing pressure, and the hot flames become dimmer with 
increasing pressure. At 1.0 atm and below there is a prolonged period of coolflame burning that ends with cool-flame extinc-
tion at a finite droplet size; the cool-flame-extinction droplet diameter increases and the cool-flame burning rate decreases 
with decreasing ambient pressure. Above 1.25 atm warm-flame burning and hot-flame re-ignitions become prevalent. At 
5.0 atm, there is no abrupt hot-flame extinction with transition to a cool flame; the flame gradually gets dimmer, and the 
flame temperature decreases over a much longer time, the transition between hot-flame and warm-flame burning becoming 
almost undiscernible.
Keywords Droplet combustion · Cool flames · Microgravity · International Space Station
Introduction
The first observations of cool flames date back to 1817 
(Davy 1817). Subsequent to the initial discovery of cool 
flames, cool flame research advanced owing to the impor-
tance of low-temperature chemistry in engines, and in 
particular, engine knock. Advanced engine concepts such 
as homogeneous charge compression ignition (HCCI) and 
reactivity controlled compression ignition (RCCI) engines 
have the potential for increased efficiency and reduced 
emissions by increasing operating pressures and lowering 
operating temperatures; placing more importance on a pre-
dictive understanding of low-temperature chemical kinetics. 
Traditionally most cool-flame research utilized premixed Timmothy Krause, Vedha Nayagam, Tanvir Farouk, Frederick Dryer

fuel/air mixtures in static (e.g., Mallard and Le Chatelier 
1880) and flow (e.g., Dryer and Glassman 1973) reactors, 
rapid compression machines (e.g., Sung and Curran 2014) 
and shock tubes (e.g., Hanson and Davidson 2014; Herbon 
et al. 2002). An important concept in cool-flame research 
is the presence of the negative temperature coefficient 
(NTC) regime where, at an intermediate temperature range 
between the cold starting condition and the hot-flame tem-
perature, the overall reactivity (heat release) decreases with 
increasing temperature.
As highlighted by Law and Faeth (Law and Faeth 1994), 
reduced-gravity studies offer geometric simplification (e.g., 
1-D flames), and no buoyant flows which allow the study of 
weak, near-limit flames which include cool flames. Kumagai 
and Isoda (1956) were the first to realize the advantages 
of the microgravity environment experimentally by study -
ing spherically-symmetric droplet combustion in a one sec-
ond drop tower at the University of Tokyo. Pearlman and 
co-workers (Fairlie et al. 2005; Foster and Pearlman 2006; 
Pearlman 2000), however, were the first to recognize the 
potential for microgravity studies to provide a window into 
cool flame research by eliminating the buoyancy-induced 
flows associated with the low-temperature heat release. The 
authors used a static reactor and showed how the buoyant 
flows changes both the flame shape and evolution and cool-
flame induction time.
Prior to 2012 most droplet combustion research in 
microgravity involved the ignition, burning and extinction 
of ‘hot flames’, with flame temperatures greater than or 
equal to approximately 1200 K (e.g., Nayagam et al. 1998). 
There was a limited amount of research that examined 
low-temperature chemistry during two-stage ignition of 
isolated droplets in ambient temperatures below about 900 K 
(Tanabe et al. 1995). Studies of large alkane droplets in a 
long-duration experiment (FlammabilityLimit-Experiment, 
FLEX) on the International Space Station (ISS) showed, for 
the first time, quasi-steady droplet combustion sustained 
by a low temperature or cool flame (Nayagam et al. 2012; 
Farouk and Dryer  2014; Cuoci et al. 2013). This cool-
flame supported droplet burning is possible because of the 
existence of the NTC regime.
Following the discovery of cool-flame burning in the ISS 
experiments Ju and coworkers were able to sustain steady 
cool flames in terrestrial laboratory studies using a counter-
flow burner. The initial experiments (Reuter et al. 2016, 
2017a) used dimethyl ether (DME) and ozone to promote the 
low-temperature burning. Subsequent experiments, however, 
used alkane fuels, first with ozone in the oxidizer stream 
and finally with no ozone (Reuter et al. 2017b) to produce a 
cool diffusion flame. Unlike the ISS experiments that have 
limited resources (i.e., test points and test time), these ter -
restrial counter-flow experiments provided a detailed flam-
mability map for cool flames across a wide range of fuels 
and ambient conditions (Reuter et al. 2017b). These observa-
tions of stable cool diffusion flames have given researchers 
a wealth of insights into cool flame behavior and led to an 
improved predictive capability of cool-flame behavior; these 
insights compiled and summarized in recent review articles 
(Ju 2021; Ju et al. 2019).
Cool-flame droplet burning in the FLEX experiments 
occurred when the hot-flame (ignited by a heated wire) 
surrounding a large alkane fuel droplet extinguished when 
the radiative loss from the flame reduced the temperature 
below that required to sustain combustion (e.g., Dietrich 
et al. 2014; Nayagam et al. 1998; Marchese et al. 1999). 
This hot-flame extinction then led to a prolonged period of 
quasi-steady low-temperature burning characterized by a 
linear d-squared (droplet-diameter-time) regression and a 
near-constant flame-standoff ratio (Farouk and Dryer 2014; 
Nayagam et al. 2016). Subsequent FLEX experiments 
showed that the hot flame is not strictly necessary to 
achieve cool-flame burning; the cool flame ignition can 
occur by raising the flash point of the fuel using a much 
lower ignition energy so as to not overheat the liquid and 
produce a significant diffusive fuel vapor/air layer around 
the droplet (Farouk et al. 2017 ). The FLEX experiments 
further showed that the cool flame burns only a fraction 
of the vaporized fuel, and the unburned fuel re-condenses 
far outside the flame zone to form a large vapor cloud that 
is visible on both a backlit view of the droplet and a color 
camera view of the experiment (Dietrich et al. 2017a, b). 
When the droplet becomes small enough, the cool flame 
extinguishes, a process that is characterized by a plateau in 
the droplet regression history and rapid condensation of the 
remaining fuel vapor (Nayagam et al. 2015).
The FLEX experiments also showed the significant influ-
ence of pressure on cool-flame droplet burning. The first 
experiments at hyperbaric pressures and related numerical 
modeling showed that, in carbon-dioxide-diluted atmos-
pheres, the cool flame could spontaneously re-ignite a hot 
flame that would subsequently extinguish and initiate further 
cool-flame burning, a process that could repeat itself multi-
ple times (Farouk et al. 2015). Subsequent experiments and 
numerical modeling showed that this process can occur at 
lower pressures and does not require ambient carbon diox-
ide (Dietrich et al. 2017a, b; Farouk and Dryer 2022). Fur-
ther FLEX experiments and companion modeling (Farouk 
et al. 2019) with n-heptane fuel droplets at elevated (3 atm) 
pressure in helium-diluted ambient environments found 
that following hot-flame extinction the flame transitions to 
a ‘warm-flame’ burning mode where the flame temperature 
is around 970 K for a short period, and then moves into 
a ‘cool-flame’ mode with a lower flame temperature (∼ 
765 K). Independently Ju and co-workers (Yehia et al. 2018, 
2019) also showed the existence of warm diffusion flames 
on experiments with their counter-flow burner.

This article presents experimental results of the Cool-
Flames-Investigation (CFI) experiments aboard the ISS that 
studied the low-temperature droplet burning in more detail. 
The experiments used a new camera system to visualize the 
cool flame, a variable-gain radiometer, and different fuels 
and fuel mixtures. The test conditions focused on oxygen/
nitrogen mixtures over a range of pressures, including 
a limited number of tests at the same oxygen index but 
with helium replacing some of the inert (nitrogen). The 
present paper summarizes all of the experimental results 
for n-dodecane in oxygen/nitrogen ambients. Farouk 
and Dryer (2022) presented some of the data earlier in 
numerical modeling and analyses of hot- and cool-flame 
burning and extinction phenomena; this work emphasizes 
the experimental observations and includes radiometer and 
sooting data not yet available in the literature.
Experimental Apparatus and Data Analysis
The experiments used the Multi-User Droplet Combustion 
Apparatus (MDCA) that is an insert to the Combustion Inte-
grated Rack (CIR), a full-sized rack inside the Destiny mod-
ule of the ISS. The hardware and software are identical to 
that in previous publications (Dietrich et al. 2014, 2015a, 
b), except for some important differences. The field-of-view 
(FOV) of the backlit images of the droplet was increased to 
approximately 5 cm × 5 cm but used the same image array 
(1024 × 1024 pixels). This resulted in slightly less spatial res-
olution but increased the likelihood that a free-floating drop-
let would stay in the FOV. The recent experiments also used 
a new intensified camera (12-bit, 1392 × 1040 monochrome 
pixel array) equipped with a filter wheel and an increased 
FOV (90 mm × 68 mm). For the hot-flame burning period 
a filter wheel rotates to place a narrowband 430 nm filter in 
front of the camera and lens to visualize the CH∗ chemilumi-
nescence. When the radiometer detects hot-flame extinction, 
the filter wheel rotates to put a wideband (390–490 nm) filter 
in front of the camera so that it can detect the formaldehyde 
chemiluminescence from the cool flame.
There was a protection system for the camera that shut 
down the intensifier when the camera and radiometer 
detected a hot-flame re-ignition during cool-flame burning. 
This system worked quite well at lower pressures. At higher 
ambient pressures, however, it became more complex as the 
hot flames became dimmer, the warm flames brighter and 
re-ignitions were frequent and unpredictable. As a result 
there were periods of the test where there was no image 
data from the intensified camera because either the wrong 
filter was in place and/or the camera shut down because of 
a hot-flame re-ignition.
The droplets in the previous FLEX experiments were 
primarily free-floated in the chamber. Some experiments, 
however, ‘tethered’ the droplet to an 80 µm silicon-carbide 
(SiC) fiber to maintain all of the events within the FOV of 
all of the cameras. This tethering significantly increased the 
likelihood of a successful test, but led to perturbations in the 
burning process, especially at small droplet diameters, such 
as near cool-flame extinction. To further reduce perturba-
tions to the burning process, the present experiments used a 
smaller 40 µm carbide fiber to tether the droplet.
To improve flame radiation observations, the fixed-gain 
amplification used in the prior FLEX experiments was 
replaced by a variable-gain amplifier to better resolve the 
flame radiance during both the hot-flame and cool-flame 
burning periods. This modification was especially important 
for recording the narrowband radiometer observations (look-
ing at water vapor emission in the 5–7 µm range) at both 
cool- and hot-flame burning conditions without saturating 
the amplifier.
Finally, software modifications were implemented to 
better control the energy supplied to the droplet during the 
ignition phase of each experiment. Whereas the previous 
ISS droplet-combustion experiments used a preset ignition 
time, the current experiments used feedback from the radi-
ometers to determine when ignition of the developing fuel 
vapor/oxidizer layer occurred. Once the radiometer detected 
flame initiation, the control computer turned off the ignit-
ers and retracted them from the droplet automatically. The 
radiometer values chosen to indicate ignition and extinction 
of the hot flame were set by the test operators prior to each 
experiment and could be changed from test to test.
The fuel for the results presented in this article was 
pure n-dodecane and the ambient gas mixtures were oxy -
gen/nitrogen (0.21/0.79 and 0.17/0.83 O 2/N2 mole frac -
tion). The ambient pressure ranged from 0.50 to 5.0 atm; 
the higher pressures representing a change from the pre-
vious FLEX experiments that were limited to 3.0 atm. In 
theory the experiments could have used droplet diameters 
from approximately 1 mm to over 7 mm based on previous 
ISS droplet combustion experiments. Droplets smaller than  
3–3.5 mm tend to burn to completion and do not exhibit  
radiative hot-flame extinction and cool-flame burning. Larger  
droplets, however, use large amounts of fuel and have very 
long test times (thus consuming large amounts of digital 
storage and requiring long downlink times). As a result, with 
a few exceptions, all of the tests used initial droplet sizes in 
the 4–5 mm range.
The cool flames from the ISS droplet combustion experi-
ments are very dim, invisible to the color video camera on 
the MDCA and barely discernible with the intensified cam-
era. The images improve with median filtering and image-
averaging over 500 ms (Nayagam et al. 2016). Automated 
image-processing procedures provide a measure of the flame 
diameter from a line profile across the center of the flame. 
Reported here are two relevant measures of the cool flame,
